top.line: Buyers can now send an agent, not a questionnaire
top.para: Due diligence was a spreadsheet answered by the people being asked. A buyer can now send a prompt or small agent under a behaviour policy to derive a graph of what is really in the vendor's environment, which the vendor can redact but not rewrite. Not knowing fails, and startups should double down on understandability.

s0.line: Derived graphs replace composed answers, and not knowing fails
s0.para: The form never scaled; an agent run inside the vendor's environment derives what reaches production unreviewed, what is documented and threat modelled. The test is risk-based, the behaviour policy is the due diligence document for agents, and the twist is to sell code review graphs to buyers, investors and acquirers rather than developers.

s1.line: The questionnaire got careful answers, never the facts
s1.para: The 2025 SIG has 627 core questions, and Whistic found vendors answering 37.3 requests a month at 179 hours. Tools like Vanta and Conveyor automate answers from documents, not facts. Companies compose defensible answers with room in them, but will not lie on a record.

s2.line: If a vendor can graph itself, buyers can ask
s2.para: The buyer sends a prompt and agent that the vendor runs on its own repositories under a behaviour policy, reading every file before it leaves. Three differences: the answer is derived not composed, so the vendor keeps a redaction marker but loses the pen; it costs compute not days; and the vendor should run it on itself first.

s3.line: Good questions make even silence an answer
s3.para: Admitting unreviewed code reaches production is fine with a map and mitigations; not knowing is the finding. A threat model is the fastest read of whether a team knows what it protects, and tracing the last fifty bugs separates reviewed from generated-code failures. The result must be a graph, because "lack of evidence is evidence".

s4.line: Enough review depends on what the software can do
s4.para: None of this is a purity test. A startup admitting generated, non-mission-critical code with mitigations passes, while the same sentence from a vendor holding customer data is the finding. The agent shows the gap between what a product is sold as and what its practices are fit for, making compliance genuinely risk-based.

s5.line: A behaviour policy shows buyers an agent's blast radius
s5.para: Agent behaviour policies state identity, permissions, approvals and accepted risks, so a buyer can read the blast radius, see which controls are enforced and which are wishes, and what risk was accepted on its behalf. A vendor with agents in the pipeline and no policy to show has said the most.

s6.line: Buyers with agents are the consequence skipped review lacked
s6.para: Companies skipping review accumulate invisible liability: Sonar found only 48% always verify AI code, Apiiro found 10 times more security issues, and Replit and Amazon incidents followed. Acquirers' snapshot scans miss practice. A startup should double down on understandability, because it has the same tools and less code to understand.

s7.line: Regulation creates duties before it creates visibility
s7.para: SBOM rules from Executive Order 14028 and CISA list components, not review. The Cyber Resilience Act fines misleading information, and the Product Liability Directive, applying from 9 December 2026, presumes defect when a vendor cannot disclose evidence. PCI DSS 6.2.3, SOC 2 CC8.1 and ISO 27001 already require review; the agent tests whether the yes was composed.

s8.line: Sell the code review company to buyers, not developers
s8.para: The previous article's design stands, but developers have just been told they do not need review. Buyers have a reason to use the same graphs, framed as due diligence, and vendors receiving the agent will run it on themselves first. It is the same company with a different first customer.

s9.line: The agent does not exist yet, only its pieces
s9.para: The graphs, behaviour policies, vaults with read keys and the previous article exist; assembling them into an acceptable prompt and policy is the next build. It should run first against this site's own repository with results published. The real uncertainty is whether buyers will ask before regulators make them, and the guess is yes.

s11.line: Sources: the memo, regulations, surveys and incident reports
s11.para: Sources include the 5 October 2026 voice memo, Dinis Cruz on threat models and the SG/Send team briefs. Also Executive Order 14028, NTIA and CISA SBOM guidance, the Cyber Resilience Act, the Product Liability Directive, PCI DSS, SOC 2, ISO 27001, and studies from Sonar, Qodo, Veracode, GitClear, Apiiro, DORA and Black Duck.
